Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

SecurityEvent

status: experimental
description: |

references:

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] TSDProxy x-tsdproxy-auth-token leaked to backend in upstream HTTP requests · [LLM] TSDProxy management-port replay: loopback connection to 127.0.0.1:8080 by non-proxy process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy management API abuse: /api/v1 request with forged x-tsdproxy-id and auth token
TSDProxy x-tsdproxy-auth-token leaked to backend in upstream HTTP requests AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for TSDProxy's internal management secret (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) appearing in HTTP requests reaching proxied backend services. When identityHeaders is enabled (the default in vulnerable builds < 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e), the token is forwarded unconditionally to every upstream, exposing it to any compromised or malicious backend for later replay. Presence of this header at a backend IS the exposure indicator; after patching/sanitisation it should never appear. Rationale: Keys on the exact secret-bearing header string 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token' named in the advisory; its arrival at any backend means the deployment is running the vulnerable unconditional-forwarding path. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because HTTP request headers are not captured in EDR process/network telemetry — this must come from proxy/web/app logs. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory Database and CVEReports for GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8 • https://almeidapaulopt.github.io/tsdproxy/docs/advanced/tailscale/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Any vulnerable-but-unattacked TSDProxy deployment with identityHeaders=true will emit this header on ALL upstream requests — expected until patched or identityHeaders:false is set
  • Backends that intentionally log full request headers for debugging (e.g. a /debug/headers reflection endpoint) surface the value in benign traffic
  • Load-test or synthetic-monitoring traffic replaying captured requests that still contain the header
  • Log-forwarders duplicating the same request across multiple sourcetypes inflating counts
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "/debug/headers"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the TSDProxy version and whether identityHeaders is enabled; if version < 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e the header exposure is inherent, not necessarily active abuse. Identify which backend(s) received the token. Step 2 (contain): Set identityHeaders:false or upgrade to the patched pseudo-version that strips HeaderAuthToken; rotate the TSDProxy management token/process. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to loopback connections to 127.0.0.1:8080 and any /api/v1/ management calls carrying a forged x-tsdproxy-id from the exposed backend to confirm whether the token was actually replayed.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"

TSDProxy management-port replay: loopback connection to 127.0.0.1:8080 by non-proxy process AIExploitation High
Detects a backend/host process opening a connection to the TSDProxy management port (127.0.0.1:8080) when that process is not tsdproxy itself. This is the replay step of GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8: a compromised backend that captured x-tsdproxy-auth-token connects from localhost to the management API to impersonate an arbitrary Tailscale identity. Legitimate management traffic arrives over the tailnet, not loopback from a non-proxy binary. Rationale: Uses the exact management endpoint from the advisory's repro (127.0.0.1:8080) plus exclusion of the legitimate tsdproxy binary — a loopback connection to that port from any other process is the concrete replay behaviour. Sentinel/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: process-attributed loopback connections live in EDR (DeviceNetworkEvents/FDR/Sysmon), not in Sentinel's ASIM network appliance tables or AWS CloudTrail. Corroborated via GitLab Advisory Database. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Local monitoring/health-check agents (curl, wget, blackbox_exporter) probing the management port on 127.0.0.1:8080 for liveness
  • An administrator using curl/httpie locally to query the management API for legitimate operations
  • Another service coincidentally bound to or reaching 8080 on loopback on a shared host
  • Container orchestrator readiness probes hitting the port over loopback in host-network mode
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl","wget","blackbox_exporter","kubelet") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process/binary and account; determine whether it is a known monitoring agent or an unexpected backend/shell process. Inspect the command line for /api/v1/ and x-tsdproxy-id references. Step 2 (contain): If the process is not sanctioned, isolate the host/container, kill the process, rotate the TSDProxy management token, and set identityHeaders:false or upgrade to the patched build. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate to web/access logs for /api/v1/ requests carrying a forged x-tsdproxy-id, and review the backend for the initial code-execution vector that enabled token capture.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") and RemotePort == 8080
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessFileName) and InitiatingProcessFileName !contains "tsdproxy"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceNetworkEvents

TSDProxy management API abuse: /api/v1 request with forged x-tsdproxy-id and auth token AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the privilege-escalation payload of GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8: an HTTP request to a TSDProxy management path (/api/v1/, e.g. /api/v1/proxies) that carries both the replayed x-tsdproxy-auth-token and an attacker-chosen x-tsdproxy-id. Because ResolveWhois trusts the x-tsdproxy-id header for any localhost caller presenting a valid token, this grants full management control (enumerate proxies, pause/restart services, trigger webhook SSRF). Rationale: Combines two article-specific strings — the forged identity header x-tsdproxy-id and the management path prefix /api/v1/ (advisory repro hits /api/v1/proxies) — so it fires on the actual escalation request rather than generic proxy traffic. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: request paths and custom headers are not in EDR or CloudTrail telemetry; only proxy/app HTTP logs carry them. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory Database and CVEReports. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate TSDProxy dashboard/admin operations that internally reference x-tsdproxy-id headers in verbose logs
  • Automation or IaC tooling calling /api/v1/ management endpoints during deployment with valid Tailscale identity
  • Security scanners/pentest tooling exercising the /api/v1/ surface during an authorised assessment
  • Debug logging that echoes request headers for all traffic, surfacing x-tsdproxy-id on benign requests
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine the source of the /api/v1/ call — was it a loopback caller (matching the replay pattern) and does the x-tsdproxy-id value differ from a real tailnet identity? Note which management operations were invoked (enumerate/pause/restart/webhook). Step 2 (contain): Rotate the management token, upgrade to the patched pseudo-version 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e or set identityHeaders:false, and review configured webhook URLs for SSRF abuse. Step 3 (hunt): Tie back to UC2 (loopback 127.0.0.1:8080) and UC1 (token leak at a backend) to reconstruct the full chain, and audit proxy config/webhook delivery logs for attacker-triggered actions.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "x-tsdproxy-id" and SyslogMessage has "/api/v1/"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "x-tsdproxy-id" AND "/api/v1/"
CLOUD
index=* (sourcetype=*proxy* OR sourcetype=*access* OR sourcetype=*nginx* OR sourcetype=*tsdproxy* OR sourcetype=*syslog*) "x-tsdproxy-id" ("/api/v1/" OR "/api/v2/")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(uri_path) as paths values(src) as sources by host, sourcetype
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count

SiYuan Electron client spawns command interpreter (XSS-to-RCE via child_process) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payoff of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-44588: a stored XSS in an attribute-view cell executes in the SiYuan renderer (nodeIntegration:true) and calls require('child_process') to run native commands. A note-taking app spawning cmd/powershell/wscript is the concrete, article-specific outcome. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete RCE mechanism — Electron nodeIntegration renderer calling require('child_process') — pinned to the named parent binary SiYuan.exe. A knowledge/notes app spawning shells is near-zero baseline. Cross-checked against the SiYuan advisory, CVE-2026-39846 (same require('child_process').exec RCE pattern) and neighbor CVE-2026-44588. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-39846/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50551
ATT&CKT1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • SiYuan updater/installer spawning a helper via cmd during version upgrade
  • A user-configured export/pandoc pipeline that SiYuan launches through a shell
  • Admin manually launching SiYuan from a script that reparents a console child
  • Security tooling that reparents processes and mislabels SiYuan.exe as the parent
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\git.exe","pandoc","--update","siyuan-updater") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "SiYuan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain — benign hits are git/pandoc/updater with recognizable args; malicious hits show base64/IEX/download-cradle or `calc`/reconnaissance commands and correlate to a recently opened note with an attribute-view. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the SiYuan.exe process tree, and block outbound from any spawned child; preserve the offending data/storage/av/<avID>.json for analysis. 3) Hunt: enumerate the user's synced workspace peers (same account/sync target) for the same av JSON, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the spawned child reaching external hosts. Push SiYuan >= 3.7.0.

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: File Browser Hook-Auth Command Injection - filebrowser Spawns Shell or Recon Binary
id: 6b1f8c2a-9d3e-4f7a-8c1b-2e5a7c9d4f11
description: Detects the File Browser server binary spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child, indicative of CVE-2026-54088 pre-auth command injection via the authentication hook.
references:

  - https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10

  - attack.t1033
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent:

  tool_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/id'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/uname'
      - '/hostname'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'

      - '/perl'
  shell_child:
    Image|endswith:

    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/etc/passwd'
      - '/etc/shadow'

      - '$('
  condition: parent and (tool_child or (shell_child and shell_markers))
level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^filebrowser$/i
| (ImageFileName=/\/(id|whoami|uname|hostname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|python[0-9]?|perl|ruby|php)$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|ash|zsh|ksh)$/i AND regex("(/etc/passwd|/etc/shadow|whoami|uname|/dev/tcp/|;|\\$\\()", field=CommandLine)))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="filebrowser" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh") AND (Processes.process="*/etc/passwd*" OR Processes.process="*/etc/shadow*" OR Processes.process="*whoami*" OR Processes.process="*uname*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp/*" OR Processes.process="*;*" OR Processes.process="*`*" OR Processes.process="*$(*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="filebrowser" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh") AND (Processes.process="*/etc/passwd*" OR Processes.process="*/etc/shadow*" OR Processes.process="*whoami*" OR Processes.process="*uname*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp/*" OR Processes.process="*;*" OR Processes.process="*`*" OR Processes.process="*$(*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FileBrowser proxy-auth header forgery naming admin on /api/login · [LLM] FileBrowser identity-cycling: 3+ user identities from one untrusted source in 5 min
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FileBrowser auto-account-creation: first-seen username in proxy auth header
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] FileBrowser post-bypass admin API actions (DELETE/PUT /api/users, /api/settings) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
FileBrowser reverse-proxy bypass: direct external access to exposed port 8085 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound connections that reach the FileBrowser container port (published as 8085 via Docker -p 8085:80) directly from a public/untrusted source, bypassing the reverse proxy (nginx/Traefik/Caddy) that is the sole security boundary for auth.method=proxy. Because auth/proxy.go has zero origin validation, any client that can reach the port directly can forge the X-Remote-User header, so a direct external hit on the exposed port is the network pre-condition for CVE-2026-54089 exploitation. Rationale: Article states exploitation requires an attacker who 'can reach the server directly' and cites Docker '-p 8085:80' publishing to 0.0.0.0; a direct public hit on 8085 is the network pre-condition for the header-forgery bypass. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory and the auth/proxy.go root-cause writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-54089
ATT&CKT1190 T1199
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys/Palo Alto Expanse) probing the exposed port
  • External uptime/health-check monitors (Pingdom, UptimeRobot) hitting the port for availability
  • A sysadmin intentionally reaching the port directly for debugging as described in the article
  • Cloud load-balancer or NAT gateway health probes that appear as public IPs
  • Security team's own external attack-surface scans
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileBrowser instance runs auth.method=proxy and that 8085 is meant to be proxy-only; identify the reverse-proxy egress IP set and check whether SourceIP is outside it. 2) Contain: firewall/security-group the container port to the reverse proxy IP only (bind 127.0.0.1 or restrict inbound), and rotate the JWT signing key to invalidate any minted tokens. 3) Hunt: pull FileBrowser/WAF logs for /api/login requests from the same SourceIP carrying an X-Remote-User header and for any user accounts created in the last 30 days (auto-creation primitive).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8085                       // FileBrowser container port from -p 8085:80
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8085                  // FileBrowser exposed container port
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","accept","allowed")
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser proxy-auth header forgery naming admin on /api/login AIExploitation High
Hunts POST /api/login requests carrying a proxy-auth identity header (X-Remote-User / X-Forwarded-User / X-Authenticated-User / X-Auth) whose value names an administrative account (admin/administrator/root) while originating from outside the trusted reverse-proxy egress range. Because ProxyAuth.Auth() trusts the header with no origin/secret check, a forged admin header from a non-proxy source is the direct signature of the CVE-2026-54089 authentication bypass and full admin takeover. Rationale: Uses the exact attack primitive from the PoC: a forged X-Remote-User (configurable via auth.header; ecosystem defaults are X-Remote-User / X-Forwarded-User per FileBrowser docs) naming 'admin' sent to /api/login. Header value + non-proxy source IP is high-fidelity because legitimate proxy traffic always originates from the proxy egress IP and the proxy sets the header itself. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch blank: HTTP request headers are not present in EDR or CloudTrail telemetry — this needs a WAF/proxy that logs request headers. Cross-checked against GHSA advisory, auth/proxy.go lines 21-28, and filebrowser.org/authentication.html. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html
ATT&CKT1548 T1556 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A misconfigured second reverse proxy not in the known egress allowlist forwarding legitimate SSO traffic
  • Penetration testers / red team validating the CVE from an internal-but-non-proxy host
  • A legitimate admin whose real username is literally 'admin' logging in through a newly-added proxy node
  • WAF logging the header on blocked (not forwarded) requests during tuning
  • Automated config-management tooling hitting /api/login with a service header
Suppression filter
| where tolower(ProxyUser) in ("admin","administrator","root") and ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is not a sanctioned reverse-proxy egress IP; if it is not, treat as a live bypass — a valid admin JWT was almost certainly minted. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter, restrict the FileBrowser port to proxy-only, rotate the JWT signing secret to revoke issued tokens, and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: enumerate all FileBrowser user accounts (auto-creation may have added attacker-named users), review /api/settings and /api/users changes and any file download/exec activity from the same session, and audit for non-admin X-Remote-User values from the same source.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/login"
| where RequestContext has_any ("X-Remote-User", "X-Forwarded-User", "X-Authenticated-User", "X-WebAuth-User", "REMOTE_USER", "X-Auth-User")   // proxy-auth identity header
| extend ProxyUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:X-Remote-User|X-Forwarded-User|X-Authenticated-User|X-WebAuth-User|REMOTE_USER|X-Auth-User)\s*[:=]\s*([^\s;,]+)", 1, RequestContext)
| where tolower(ProxyUser) in ("admin","administrator","root")     // privileged username in forged header
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false                          // not from trusted proxy egress
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, ProxyUser
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser auto-account-creation: first-seen username in proxy auth header AIInstallation Medium
Correlates /api/login requests carrying a proxy-auth username header from an untrusted source against a 30-day baseline of previously-seen usernames, surfacing brand-new (first-seen) usernames. FileBrowser's createUser() unconditionally provisions a real account when the header names a non-existent user, giving attackers a no-authorization account-creation primitive; a first-seen username submitted from a non-proxy IP is the signature of backdoor account provisioning. Rationale: Targets the article's second primitive: 'specifying a non-existent username causes the server to automatically create a new user account.' A first-seen X-Remote-User value from a non-proxy IP maps directly to createUser() being triggered by an attacker-controlled header. Leftanti-join against a 30-day baseline expresses first-seen without ML. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch blank: request-header username is only visible in WAF/proxy logs, not EDR/CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine onboarding of a new employee whose SSO username is passed for the first time through a proxy node not yet in the trusted list
  • A newly-provisioned reverse proxy whose egress IP has not been added to the private/allowlist ranges
  • Baseline gap: usernames legitimately used before the 30-day window appearing 'first-seen'
  • Service accounts or automation logging in via a header for the first time after a config change
  • WAF header-parsing quirks that extract a truncated username value
Suppression filter
| where ProxyUser !in~ ("guest","anonymous","health","healthcheck","monitor","probe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list current FileBrowser accounts and compare against the first-seen ProxyUser value; a matching newly-created account confirms the auto-creation primitive fired. 2) Contain: delete the attacker-provisioned account(s), restrict the port to proxy-only, and rotate the JWT signing secret. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account's default permissions include execute/create/modify (article notes Defaults.Apply may grant these), inspect file operations and command execution tied to that username, and search for additional first-seen usernames from the same SourceIP.
let Baseline = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where RequestURL has "/api/login"
    | extend ProxyUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:X-Remote-User|X-Forwarded-User|X-Authenticated-User|X-WebAuth-User|REMOTE_USER|X-Auth-User)\s*[:=]\s*([^\s;,]+)", 1, RequestContext)
    | where isnotempty(ProxyUser)
    | summarize by tolower(ProxyUser);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/login"
| extend ProxyUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:X-Remote-User|X-Forwarded-User|X-Authenticated-User|X-WebAuth-User|REMOTE_USER|X-Auth-User)\s*[:=]\s*([^\s;,]+)", 1, RequestContext)
| where isnotempty(ProxyUser)
| extend ProxyUser = tolower(ProxyUser)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on ProxyUser        // first-seen username only
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, ProxyUser
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/login*" Web.http_method=POST Web.src_category!=proxy by Web.user, Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-1d") | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/login*" Web.http_method=POST Web.src_category!=proxy by Web.user, Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-1d") | sort - firstTime
FileBrowser post-bypass admin API actions (DELETE/PUT /api/users, /api/settings) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts privileged FileBrowser REST API calls — DELETE/PUT/POST against /api/users, /api/settings and /api/resources — originating from outside the trusted reverse-proxy egress range. After forging an admin JWT via the header bypass, an attacker uses these admin endpoints to modify settings, create/delete users, and manipulate files; admin-verb API traffic from a non-proxy source is the post-compromise action signature of CVE-2026-54089. Rationale: Maps to the article's outcome: a minted admin JWT (perm.admin:true) grants full control, and the PoC shows admin API calls such as GET /api/settings. This UC widens to the state-changing admin verbs an attacker would issue post-bypass. Source-IP restriction to non-proxy origins keeps fidelity. Header-level context isn't required, so this is expressible on standard proxy/webserver access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/
ATT&CKT1548 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin performing settings/user management through a proxy node not in the allowlist
  • Automated backup/config tooling issuing PUT /api/settings on a schedule
  • A monitoring integration polling /api/resources
  • Red-team/pentest validation of the CVE
  • New reverse-proxy egress IP not yet added to the private/allowlist ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SourceIP is non-proxy; correlate to any preceding /api/login with an X-Remote-User admin header from the same IP to confirm the bypass chain. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, restrict the port to proxy-only, rotate the JWT signing secret, and snapshot current FileBrowser settings/users for forensics. 3) Hunt: diff /api/settings and user list against last-known-good, review file resource operations (downloads/deletes) from the session, and check for command execution if the compromised/created account has the execute permission.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in~ ("DELETE","PUT","POST")
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/users", "/api/settings", "/api/resources")
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false                 // not from trusted proxy egress
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser identity-cycling: 3+ user identities from one untrusted source in 5 min AIExploitation High
Flags a single non-proxy source IP presenting 3 or more distinct FileBrowser user identities to the API within a 5-minute window. Legitimate proxy traffic carries one authenticated identity per user and the proxy egress IP is stable per session; rapid identity-switching from one direct source indicates the attacker is cycling forged X-Remote-User header values to impersonate multiple accounts — the 'impersonate any user' behaviour of CVE-2026-54089. Rationale: Directly implements the article's 'impersonate any user' claim: because the header is attacker-chosen with no verification, an attacker enumerating/impersonating accounts produces many distinct identities from a single direct source in a short window — a shape legitimate per-user proxy auth cannot produce. dcount over a 5-minute bin is a threshold+temporal correlation, so Sigma is skipped. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch blank: the authenticated username per web request lives in proxy/WAF logs, not EDR or CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-54089
ATT&CKT1078 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multiple real users behind a single corporate NAT / CGNAT egress IP hitting FileBrowser (if that egress isn't classified as proxy)
  • A VPN concentrator or shared jump host from which several admins legitimately work
  • Automated test suites iterating multiple test users against the API
  • A load/perf test cycling synthetic accounts
  • Mobile users sharing a carrier-grade NAT address
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the Users set from the flagged SrcIpAddr — presence of admin/root alongside several unrelated usernames strongly indicates impersonation cycling; confirm the IP is not a sanctioned NAT/proxy egress. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, restrict the FileBrowser port to proxy-only, and rotate the JWT signing secret to void all forged tokens. 3) Hunt: for each impersonated username, review file downloads/deletes and settings/user changes in the same window, and check whether any of those identities were auto-created (never existed before).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "/api/"
| where isnotempty(SrcUsername)
| where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) == false
| summarize DistinctUsers = dcount(SrcUsername), Users = make_set(SrcUsername, 20), Requests = count()
          by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctUsers >= 3          // 3+ identities from one non-proxy IP in 5 min = header cycling, not legit multi-user
| order by DistinctUsers desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Web.user) as distinct_users, values(Web.user) as users, count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/*" Web.src_category!=proxy by _time span=5m, Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where distinct_users >= 3 | sort - distinct_users
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Web.user) as distinct_users, values(Web.user) as users, count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/*" Web.src_category!=proxy by _time span=5m, Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where distinct_users >= 3 | sort - distinct_users
FileBrowser instance configured with auth.method=proxy (exploitable-config exposure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces FileBrowser processes started with proxy authentication enabled (auth.method=proxy plus an auth.header such as X-Remote-User), which is the precondition that makes CVE-2026-54089 exploitable. This is a proactive exposure hunt on endpoint process telemetry to inventory at-risk hosts before, or independently of, any live exploitation — pair the results with the direct-external-access UC to prioritise instances that are both proxy-auth and network-exposed. Rationale: Article states the vuln is 'NOT exploitable on default configuration' and requires auth.method=proxy with an auth.header (default X-Remote-User); inventorying processes launched with these flags directly enumerates exploitable hosts. Uses the exact config tokens (auth.method, auth.header, X-Remote-User) and the filebrowser binary name. Defender/Falcon/ImProcessCreate are viable because this is host process telemetry, not HTTP. CloudWatch blank: not AWS-native. NOTE flags the coverage gap for env-var/config-file deployments where flags aren't on the command line. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A correctly-hardened instance bound to 127.0.0.1 behind a proxy that strips client headers (proxy-auth enabled but not exploitable)
  • Non-production/test FileBrowser instances intentionally running proxy auth
  • A container image rebuild re-launching the same safe config repeatedly
  • Config-management (Ansible/Helm) restarts re-emitting the same flags
  • Legacy proxy-auth deployment already firewalled at the network layer
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host, determine the listen bind address (127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0) and whether the port is reachable from untrusted networks — correlate with the direct-external-access UC. 2) Contain: for exposed instances, restrict the port to the reverse-proxy egress only and configure the proxy to strip/overwrite the identity header on inbound client requests. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-exposed hosts, pull proxy/WAF logs for /api/login requests carrying X-Remote-User from non-proxy sources and audit the FileBrowser user list for accounts created via the auto-creation primitive.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "filebrowser"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "proxy"
      and (ProcessCommandLine has "auth.method" or ProcessCommandLine has "--auth.header" or ProcessCommandLine has "X-Remote-User")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// NOTE: only catches flag-based config; env-var (FB_AUTH_METHOD) or config.json/DB config will not appear in cmdline
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "proxy"
      and (TargetProcessCommandLine has "auth.method" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "auth.header" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "X-Remote-User")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SiYuan kernel config (conf.json) written — audit for empty/missing AccessAuthCode · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] External browser process connects to SiYuan kernel loopback admin port 127.0.0.1:6806 · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Browser extension manifest rewritten adding networking/host permissions (supply-chain) · Suspicious browser extension installation

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
External browser process connects to SiYuan kernel loopback admin port 127.0.0.1:6806 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a Chrome/Chromium/Edge browser process opening a loopback connection to the SiYuan Note kernel HTTP server on port 6806. Per CVE-2026-54069 the kernel blanket-trusts any `chrome-extension://` Origin as RoleAdministrator, so a browser-context connection to 6806 (as opposed to the Electron siyuan.exe app itself) is the in-flight exploitation signal for a malicious/compromised extension exfiltrating notes or injecting stored XSS. Rationale: Uses the article's exact kernel bind address (127.0.0.1) and port (6806) plus the browser-process constraint that distinguishes a rogue extension from SiYuan's own Electron siyuan.exe process — the Origin header itself (chrome-extension://) is not carried in EDR/network telemetry so the browser-to-loopback 5-tuple is the highest-fidelity observable proxy for it. Loopback capture varies by EDR agent, hence hunting tier; Sentinel ImNetworkSession lacks process attribution so triage the host manually. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
ATT&CKT1176 T1078
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Official SiYuan web-clipper browser extension legitimately posting captures to the kernel on 6806
  • Developer or power-user testing the SiYuan API from a browser devtools/console session
  • Browser-based localhost tooling reusing port 6806
  • SiYuan run in browser (non-desktop) mode where the UI itself is a browser tab talking to 6806
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact browser process (InitiatingProcessId/CommandLine) and enumerate that user's installed extensions; confirm whether the official SiYuan web-clipper is installed and expected on this host. 2) Contain: if no sanctioned SiYuan clipper is installed, disable/remove the browser's recently-updated extensions and, if a note workspace holds sensitive data, set a non-empty AccessAuthCode in SiYuan and restart the kernel. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for subsequent connections to attacker infrastructure (stored-XSS callback like attacker.example/steal) and for conf.json writes indicating /api/system/setConf tampering.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 6806
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan kernel config (conf.json) written — audit for empty/missing AccessAuthCode AIReconnaissance Low
Config-audit hunt that surfaces writes to a SiYuan workspace conf.json so an analyst can verify the AccessAuthCode field. CVE-2026-54069 is trivially exploitable on desktop installs where AccessAuthCode defaults to an empty string, so any host running SiYuan with unset auth is exposed to unauthenticated admin API access from any browser extension. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated config surface — conf.json holding the AccessAuthCode that defaults empty on ContainerStd desktop installs. EDR file telemetry cannot read the field's value, so this is an inventory/audit pivot: every hit is a host to check manually for unset auth, hence Low confidence and hunting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
ATT&CKT1078.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine SiYuan settings changes writing conf.json during normal use
  • SiYuan data-sync/backup clients copying the workspace including conf.json
  • First-run workspace initialization creating conf.json
  • Users legitimately editing SiYuan preferences
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each returned host, open the referenced conf.json and inspect the AccessAuthCode value — empty string, null, or missing = exposed. 2) Contain: for exposed hosts holding sensitive notes, direct the owner to set a strong AccessAuthCode and upgrade SiYuan past the fixed kernel version (>= 0.0.0-20260628153353-2d5d72223df4). 3) Hunt: on any host confirmed exposed, review for browser-to-127.0.0.1:6806 connections (UC1) and outbound connections to unfamiliar domains indicating prior data exfiltration via /api/query/sql.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "conf.json"
| where FolderPath has "siyuan"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "conf.json"
| where TargetFilePath has "siyuan"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser extension manifest rewritten adding networking/host permissions (supply-chain) AIInstallation Low
Hunts writes to Chrome/Edge/Brave extension manifest.json or the profile Preferences/Secure Preferences files — the artifacts rewritten when an installed extension is updated with new permissions. CVE-2026-54069 is amplified by a supply-chain model where a previously-benign extension pushes a malicious update; because localhost:6806 is reachable with zero declared host_permissions, watch specifically for extension permission/manifest churn preceding the loopback abuse in UC1. Rationale: Grounded in the article's supply-chain amplification note ('a single compromised popular Chrome extension update can silently exploit every SiYuan desktop user') and the fact that the PoC extension needs zero host_permissions — so any manifest/permission churn on a Chromium profile is the earliest artifact of a weaponized update. High FP because browsers legitimately update extensions; best used chained with UC1 (same host, followed by a 6806 loopback connection). Sentinel path uses ImFileEvent (not the Defender-only DeviceRegistryEvents) to stay schema-valid. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome/Edge silently auto-updating installed extensions in the background
  • User manually installing or updating a browser extension
  • Enterprise force-installed (ExtensionInstallForcelist) extension deployment
  • New browser profile creation writing fresh Preferences/manifest files
  • Browser sync reconciling extension state across devices
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which extension ID's manifest changed and diff old vs new permissions (look for newly added networking, <all_urls>, or host permissions); check the extension's reputation and update timestamp. 2) Contain: if the extension is unsanctioned or the update is unexpected, disable/remove it via browser management policy across affected hosts. 3) Hunt: on the same host/user, correlate within a short window for a browser connection to 127.0.0.1:6806 (UC1) and for outbound C2/exfil connections, confirming the update was weaponized against a running SiYuan kernel.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("manifest.json","Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\BraveSoftware\", @"\Chromium\User Data\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("manifest.json","Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\BraveSoftware\", @"\Chromium\User Data\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Authorizer /authorize implicit-flow token leak to off-origin redirect_uri (CVE-2026-54072) AIExploitation High
Hunts exploitation of CVE-2026-54072: /authorize requests using response_type=token or id_token whose redirect_uri points at a host different from the Authorizer server, causing access_token/id_token/refresh_token to be appended to a 302 redirect toward an attacker-controlled URL. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable route (/authorize), the exact implicit-flow trigger values (response_type=token / id_token), and the redirect_uri host != server host mismatch that is the CWE-601 root cause. Cross-checked GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv, the GitLab advisory, and sibling GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SPA OAuth client registered with an implicit-flow callback on a partner/CDN domain distinct from the Authorizer host
  • Internal test/staging automation exercising the implicit flow across environment hostnames
  • Mobile app custom-scheme callbacks that regex-parse as a different host
  • A reverse proxy rewriting Host header so ServerHost != registered origin
  • DAST scanners probing the OAuth endpoint
Suppression filter
| where tolower(RedirectHost) != tolower(HttpHostName) and RedirectHost !in~ ("partner-callback.example.com", "login.mycdn.example.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: url-decode redirect_uri per hit; confirm the host is external/attacker-controlled and response_type is token/id_token with a 302 response. 2) Contain: confirm Authorizer >= 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d; else add AllowedOrigins/WAF enforcement on /authorize and revoke refresh tokens for victims. 3) Hunt: review /userinfo and downstream API calls under stolen bearer tokens; pivot the off-origin host across oauth_login, verify_email, magic_link_login, forgot_password.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)response_type(=|%3D)(id_)?token"
| extend RedirectRaw = extract(@"(?i)redirect_uri(?:=|%3D)([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectDecoded = url_decode(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectHost = extract(@"(?i)https?://([^/:?]+)", 1, RedirectDecoded)
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost) and tolower(RedirectHost) != tolower(HttpHostName)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ServerHost = HttpHostName, RedirectHost, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Authorizer OAuth2 implicit-flow token leak via off-origin redirect_uri (CVE-2026-54072)

description: Detects /authorize requests using implicit-flow response_type=token or id_token combined with an off-origin redirect_uri, the exploitation shape of CVE-2026-54072 in authorizerdev/authorizer.

Authorizer unauthenticated /graphql client_id reconnaissance (CVE-2026-54072 pre-exploit) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the recon step of CVE-2026-54072 where an unauthenticated attacker queries public /graphql with {meta{client_id}} to harvest the client_id needed for the malicious /authorize link. Surfaces meta/client_id introspection and single-source /graphql bursts. Rationale: Uses the article's Step-1 recon primitive ({meta{client_id}} against /graphql). POST bodies aren't in access logs, so it catches the GET-introspection variant directly and flags single-source burst volume as a proxy for the POST sweep. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv
ATT&CKT1592.004 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorizer's own front-end calling /graphql for meta/client_id on page load from CDN egress IPs
  • GraphQL IDE / schema-introspection developer tools
  • Uptime/health monitors polling /graphql
  • API gateway aggregating many users behind one IP inflating the burst
  • POST-based real recon is invisible (body not logged) and will be missed
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm introspection hits carried no Authorization header/cookie and returned 200; for bursts, distinguish known front-end/CDN egress from unfamiliar IP/ASN. 2) Contain: block unauthorized source IP/ASN at WAF, treat client_id as public, prioritise patching /authorize. 3) Hunt: correlate recon source/time with subsequent /authorize implicit-flow (UC1) and the sibling handlers oauth_login/verify_email/magic_link_login/forgot_password.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/graphql"
| extend GetIntrospection = iff(Url has "meta" and Url has "client_id", 1, 0)
| summarize Requests=count(), IntrospectionHits=sum(GetIntrospection), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode,5), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,3), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, ServerHost = HttpHostName
| where IntrospectionHits > 0 or Requests >= 20
| order by IntrospectionHits desc, Requests desc

Authorizer /authorize redirect_uri iteration — multiple distinct targets from one source AIExploitation Medium
Detects an attacker iterating CVE-2026-54072 by issuing /authorize requests with 3+ distinct redirect_uri hosts from one source IP within 5 minutes — probing which attacker-controlled domain succeeds. Legit clients use a fixed callback host. Rationale: Article notes the attacker may try multiple attacker-controlled domains/subdomains. Distinct redirect_uri hosts per source per 5-minute bucket vs the fixed-callback baseline cleanly isolates iteration/probing. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multi-tenant/white-label deployment where one gateway drives OAuth for several apps each with its own callback host
  • QA/DAST fuzzing redirect_uri across environments
  • CDN/NAT egress IP aggregating many users
  • Load-testing tooling parameterising callback URLs
  • Browser prefetch/redirect chains generating host variants
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect RedirectHosts for the source — probing shows unrelated/new domains, legit multi-tenant shows known app domains; confirm response_type=token present. 2) Contain: WAF-block the source IP; if any host is malicious, revoke tokens for affected accounts and deny-list it. 3) Hunt: pivot each RedirectHost to victims 302'd with tokens (UC1); check DNS/TI on domains; see if the source did /graphql recon (UC2) first.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| extend RedirectRaw = extract(@"(?i)redirect_uri(?:=|%3D)([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectHost = extract(@"(?i)https?://([^/:?]+)", 1, url_decode(RedirectRaw))
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost)
| summarize DistinctRedirectHosts=dcount(RedirectHost), RedirectHosts=make_set(RedirectHost,15), AuthorizeRequests=count() by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctRedirectHosts >= 3
| order by DistinctRedirectHosts desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.uri_path="/authorize" by Web.src, Web.uri_query, _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rex field=uri_query "(?i)redirect_uri(=|%3D)(?<redirect_raw>[^&]+)"
| eval redirect_decoded=urldecode(redirect_raw)
| rex field=redirect_decoded "(?i)https?://(?<redirect_host>[^/:?]+)"
| where isnotnull(redirect_host)
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(redirect_host) as distinct_redirect_hosts values(redirect_host) as redirect_hosts count as authorize_requests by src, _time
| where distinct_redirect_hosts >= 3
| sort - distinct_redirect_hosts
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.uri_path="/authorize" by Web.src, Web.uri_query, _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rex field=uri_query "(?i)redirect_uri(=|%3D)(?<redirect_raw>[^&]+)"

| rex field=redirect_decoded "(?i)https?://(?<redirect_host>[^/:?]+)"

ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New legitimate OAuth client onboarded with a cross-domain callback causing a step-change in off-origin 302 volume
  • Marketing/SSO campaign driving a login burst through a partner callback host
  • Proxy Host-header rewriting making same-origin callbacks appear off-origin
  • Sparse baseline (low-traffic tenant) tripping the multiplier on any small burst
  • At-scale load tests or synthetic OAuth monitors
Response runbook
1) Triage: break down the anomalous hour by RedirectHost and SrcIp — one dominant host = exploitation; spread across known partner domains = benign onboarding. 2) Contain: WAF-block the destination hosts and source IPs, confirm patch >= 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d, mass-revoke refresh tokens for accounts in the window. 3) Hunt: enumerate accounts 302'd to the malicious host and review /userinfo + downstream API usage; check recon (UC2) and iteration (UC3) from the same infrastructure.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has "/authorize" and tostring(HttpStatusCode) == "302"
| extend RedirectRaw = extract(@"(?i)redirect_uri(?:=|%3D)([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectHost = extract(@"(?i)https?://([^/:?]+)", 1, url_decode(RedirectRaw))
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost) and tolower(RedirectHost) != tolower(HttpHostName)
| make-series OffOrigin302 = count() default=0 on TimeGenerated from ago(14d) to now() step 1h by ServerHost = HttpHostName
| extend (anomalies, score, baseline) = series_decompose_anomalies(OffOrigin302, 3.0)
| mv-expand TimeGenerated to typeof(datetime), OffOrigin302 to typeof(long), anomalies to typeof(long), baseline to typeof(double)
| where anomalies == 1 and OffOrigin302 > 5 * baseline
| project TimeGenerated, ServerHost, OffOrigin302, baseline, score
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.uri_path="/authorize" Web.status=302 by Web.dest, Web.uri_query, _time span=1h

| rex field=uri_query "(?i)redirect_uri(=|%3D)(?<redirect_raw>[^&]+)"
| eval redirect_decoded=urldecode(redirect_raw)
| rex field=redirect_decoded "(?i)https?://(?<redirect_host>[^/:?]+)"
| where isnotnull(redirect_host) AND redirect_host!=dest
| timechart span=1h sum(count) as offorigin_302
