SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration) spawning shell/LOLBin child — XSS-to-RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-54067 (and the sibling SiYuan XSS-to-RCE bugs): a stored snippet/caption/README breaks out of its HTML context and, because the renderer runs with nodeIntegration:true, calls require('child_process') to spawn a command interpreter. A Markdown note app should essentially never parent cmd.exe/powershell.exe, so this parent->child pair is high-fidelity across the whole SiYuan RCE bug class. Rationale: Anchored on InitiatingProcessFileName=siyuan.exe (the Electron main/renderer binary confirmed in the advisory as running nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false) parenting a command interpreter — the observable end state of require('child_process').execSync from injected JS. Node's execSync on Windows spawns cmd.exe, making cmd.exe the highest-value child. Robust across all SiYuan XSS-to-RCE variants. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan document export to PDF/Word invoking a bundled pandoc/wkhtmltopdf helper (verify child binary is the export helper, not a shell)
  • User-configured 'open with' / external-command plugins in SiYuan that legitimately shell out
  • A power-user snippet the owner wrote themselves that intentionally calls a benign command (confirm with the user)
  • SiYuan auto-update or crash-reporter helper launched via cmd.exe wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("pandoc", "wkhtmltopdf", "--export", "SiYuan-Kernel"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — a benign export helper looks nothing like a shell one-liner. Check whether the same user recently edited a CSS/JS snippet or synced a workspace. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke/rotate any SiYuan Cloud / S3 / WebDAV sync credentials for that workspace so the poisoned snippet can't re-propagate. 3) HUNT: Retrieve data/snippets/conf.json from every peer that syncs the same workspace and grep for '</style>' or 'onerror='; upgrade all SiYuan clients to >=3.7.0; sweep other hosts for siyuan.exe parenting interpreters over the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "siyuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\siyuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/siyuan\.exe/i

Non-SiYuan process writing synced snippet store data\snippets\conf.json AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the plant/delivery stage of CVE-2026-54067: the malicious CSS snippet is stored in the workspace file data/snippets/conf.json, which syncs to every peer. When a process OTHER than the SiYuan kernel writes that file — e.g. a Dropbox/Syncthing/Google Drive sync client, a text editor, or a shared-drive process — it indicates the snippet store was tampered with out-of-band, exactly the 'workspace-write compromise via shared filesystem' vector the advisory calls out. Rationale: Uses the exact storage path from the advisory (data/snippets/conf.json, referenced at kernel/model/repository.go:1748,1798) and excludes the legitimate writer (the SiYuan kernel). A write by a sync client or editor is the out-of-band tamper path the advisory enumerates (Dropbox/Syncthing/network share/git). Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/
ATT&CKT1080 T1195
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dropbox.exe / SyncthingTray.exe / googledrivefs.exe legitimately syncing a workspace whose owner edited snippets on another device (benign but the exact tamper vector — inspect the resulting content)
  • A backup agent (Veeam, Duplicati, Acronis) reading/rewriting the workspace folder
  • User editing conf.json directly in VS Code / Notepad++ during troubleshooting
  • Git client (git.exe) pulling a workspace tracked in version control
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine-and-restore touching the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","duplicati.exe","backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "git.exe"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the written data/snippets/conf.json and grep for '</style>', 'onerror=', '<img', or 'child_process' — a benign sync writes normal CSS/JS. Note the writing process and account. 2) CONTAIN: If payload strings are present, quarantine the workspace, block sync (pause Dropbox/Syncthing, revoke WebDAV/S3 creds), and prevent SiYuan from loading the poisoned snippet until cleaned. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every device syncing the same workspace and check for the same conf.json write; pivot to UC #1 (siyuan.exe spawning a shell) on those hosts to see if RCE already fired; confirm all clients are >=3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\snippets\" and FileName =~ "conf.json"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe","siyuan-kernel.exe","kernel.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\snippets\" and TargetFileName =~ "conf.json"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has "siyuan")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki Bazar CalcField eval() RCE — dangerous PHP functions in form-save request AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound web requests to a YesWiki server carrying PHP execution primitives (system(), passthru(), shell_exec(), proc_open(), file_get_contents()) in the Bazar Calc-field formula — the CVE-2026-52778 regex-bypass-to-eval() vector. Article-specific because it targets the exact eval() sink and the RCE payload shape shown in the advisory (`abs(1) + system('id')`). Rationale: Anchors on the exact eval() abuse from the advisory (`system('id')` in a Bazar formula) by matching PHP command-execution functions plus a following literal or URL-encoded '(' in the request. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory Database and CVEReports which confirm unauthenticated RCE via CalcField.php formatValuesBeforeSave(). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/commit/dd2bd8fb099de0d21504bda8a810693b3fcb8e52
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different application on the same WAF legitimately passing text like 'exec(' in a code-snippet or documentation field
  • Security scanners (Nuclei/Burp) probing the site during authorized pentests
  • Developers pasting PHP snippets into a wiki page body
  • WAF already blocking the request (still logs the payload) — treat as blocked-but-attempted, not compromise
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "blocked" and DeviceAction != "deny"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target host is a YesWiki instance and check its version — if < 4.6.6 it is vulnerable. Pull the full request (body + source IP) and check WAF DeviceAction (blocked vs allowed). 2) Contain: if allowed and host is <4.6.6, block the source IP at the WAF and take the app offline or WAF-virtual-patch the Bazar save endpoint; prioritize upgrading to 4.6.6+. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint telemetry on the web host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells (UC3), new .php files under webroot (UC4), and reads of wakka.config.php/.env (UC5) around the request time.
// Point at the WAF/reverse-proxy in front of the YesWiki host. CommonSecurityLog carries the full RequestURL and, on most WAFs, the inspected body in Message/RequestContext.
let Lookback = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(system|passthru|shell_exec|proc_open|popen|exec|assert|file_get_contents|base64_decode|phpinfo)\s*(\(|%28)"
    or Message matches regex @"(?i)(system|passthru|shell_exec|proc_open|popen|file_get_contents)\s*(\(|%28)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Sample=any(RequestURL)
          by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

YesWiki CalcField ReDoS/stack-overflow DoS — deeply nested parentheses payload AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts requests to a YesWiki server containing 8+ consecutive open parentheses (literal or URL-encoded), the CVE-2026-52778 ReDoS/PCRE-stack-overflow vector that crashes the PHP-FPM/Apache worker. Article-specific: matches the advisory's exact DoS PoC of thousands of nested parens against the recursive `(?1)+` regex. Rationale: The advisory's DoS PoC is literally thousands of nested '(' chars; 8+ consecutive open-parens (raw or %28-encoded) never occurs in a genuine math formula, making this a low-FP, high-specificity match on the exact ReDoS payload. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A wiki page body legitimately containing ASCII art or deeply nested code being saved through the same host
  • Automated fuzzing/scanning during an authorized assessment
  • A poorly written legitimate math formula (rare — still worth investigating given the CVE)
  • Copy-pasted Lisp/Scheme code into a wiki field
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm host is YesWiki <4.6.6; check whether the corresponding PHP-FPM/Apache worker crashed (segfault in dmesg/apache error_log) near the request time and whether availability dropped. 2) Contain: block the source IP, and add a WAF rule rejecting requests with >6 consecutive '(' to the Bazar save endpoint; schedule the 4.6.6 upgrade which replaces the regex+eval with an AST parser. 3) Hunt: check for repeated bursts from the same source (sustained DoS) and correlate with server-health/CPU alerts and 5xx spikes.
// Deeply nested parentheses = the ReDoS/PCRE stack-overflow payload for CalcField.php. 8 chosen as a floor well above any legitimate math formula.
let Lookback = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(\(){8,}" or RequestURL matches regex @"(%28){8,}"
    or Message matches regex @"(\(){8,}" or Message matches regex @"(%28){8,}"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Sample=any(RequestURL)
          by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication
| order by Hits desc

YesWiki post-RCE — php-fpm/apache spawns Unix shell or recon binary (www-data) AIInstallation High
Detects a YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm, apache2/httpd, nginx) spawning a shell or reconnaissance binary — the observable outcome of a successful CalcField eval() RCE running as www-data. This is the strongest, lowest-FP pivot because web daemons almost never legitimately fork sh/id/whoami/curl. Rationale: A web daemon (php-fpm/apache) forking a shell or id/whoami is the canonical outcome of the article's `system('id')` RCE example and is near-zero in normal operation. Parent restricted to YesWiki web-server binaries keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/ • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate YesWiki/plugin features that shell out (e.g. thumbnail generation via ImageMagick 'convert' — not in this binary list, but custom plugins may)
  • Server monitoring/health-check scripts invoked by the web user
  • Deployment or cron tasks briefly running under the www-data account
  • A sysadmin debugging PHP with a manual `php` CLI that itself calls a shell
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "convert" and ProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — `id`/`whoami`/`uname` strongly indicate hands-on RCE validation; capture the parent php-fpm cmdline and the acting user. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and preserve the apache/php-fpm access logs mapping the request that triggered it. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on webshell writes (UC4), config/credential reads (UC5), outbound C2 from the web user, and new cron/systemd persistence created by www-data.
let Lookback = 7d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(php-fpm|php-cgi|php|httpd|apache2|nginx)"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 7d;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(php-fpm|php-cgi|/php$|httpd|apache2|nginx)"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|id|whoami|uname|curl|wget|python[0-9.]*|perl|nc|ncat)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki webshell drop — web-server process writes new .php file into webroot AIInstallation High
Detects a YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) creating a new .php file under the application tree (tools/, bazar/, files/, cache/, custom/) — the persistence step after CalcField eval() RCE. Web servers writing executable PHP is highly abnormal and article-relevant (advisory notes attackers 'inject backdoors' as www-data). Rationale: The advisory explicitly warns attackers can 'inject backdoors' as the web user; a php-fpm/apache process creating a .php file under tools/bazar/files/cache/custom is a direct, high-fidelity webshell-persistence signal specific to the YesWiki webroot layout. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/commit/dd2bd8fb099de0d21504bda8a810693b3fcb8e52
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate YesWiki updates/plugin installs performed through the web UI that write .php into custom/ or tools/
  • A YesWiki caching mechanism that materializes compiled .php templates into cache/
  • Composer/deployment running as the web user during a maintenance window
  • Theme or extension imports via the admin console
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","update","install") and FolderPath has "/cache/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the newly written .php file — look for eval/base64_decode/system/`$_POST`/`$_GET` webshell markers; note the writing process cmdline and user. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics; block the source IP identified from correlated web logs. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recently modified .php files under the webroot, check for the same content hash on other hosts, and review web logs for subsequent requests to the dropped file path.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256

let Lookback = 7d;

YesWiki credential access — web user reads wakka.config.php / .env / /etc/passwd AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the YesWiki web user (via php-fpm/apache-spawned shell) reading YesWiki's canonical secrets file wakka.config.php, a .env, or /etc/passwd/shadow using cat/grep/curl/base64 — the confidentiality-impact step the advisory calls out (reading '/etc/passwd, .env configuration files'). Product-specific because wakka.config.php holds the YesWiki DB credentials. Rationale: wakka.config.php is YesWiki's canonical config holding DB credentials; combined with the advisory's stated targets (/etc/passwd, .env) and a web-server-spawned reader binary, this captures the exact confidentiality-impact behavior for this CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin or deployment scripts running as the web user that cat/grep wakka.config.php during troubleshooting
  • Backup jobs reading .env / config files
  • Monitoring agents fingerprinting /etc/passwd
  • A developer debugging DB connectivity by grepping the config
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash)$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","deploy","monitor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain traces to php-fpm/apache (not an interactive admin shell) and check the acting user; interactive admin activity is likely benign. 2) Contain: if www-data-initiated, isolate the host, rotate the YesWiki DB credentials in wakka.config.php and any secrets in .env, and force-reset affected accounts. 3) Hunt: check for outbound exfiltration (base64/compress → DNS/HTTP egress) from the web user, correlated webshell drops (UC4), and reuse of the leaked DB credentials elsewhere.

| where FileName in~ ("cat","head","tail","less","more","grep","curl","base64","xxd","od","awk")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wakka.config.php","wakka.config",".env","/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

YesWiki CalcField exploit attempts — PHP parse/fatal errors from CalcField.php in syslog AIExploitation Low
Hunts PHP 'Parse error', 'syntax error', 'Fatal error', or 'undefined function' messages originating from CalcField.php in forwarded PHP/Apache error logs — the tell of failed regex-bypass fuzzing against the eval() sink before a working RCE payload lands. Captures attempts that succeed at hitting eval() but fail to execute cleanly. Rationale: The article's core flaw is regex-then-eval, so a bypass attempt that reaches eval() with malformed PHP produces parse/fatal errors referencing CalcField.php; clustering these errors surfaces active fuzzing that clean web-log signatures miss. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine buggy calc formula authored by a legitimate form designer producing a one-off parse error
  • A YesWiki version-mismatch/plugin bug throwing CalcField errors unrelated to attack
  • Log-noise from an unrelated PHP file that happens to reference 'CalcField' in a stack trace
  • PHP upgrade changing function availability (undefined function noise) after a maintenance window
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the surrounding error lines to recover the offending formula string and the source request/IP from correlated web logs (UC1/UC2); repeated errors from one source = active fuzzing. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and prioritize the 4.6.6 upgrade; virtual-patch the Bazar save endpoint. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint UCs (UC3/UC4/UC5) to confirm whether any attempt progressed to code execution, and review for a subsequent error-free save (the likely successful payload).

YesWiki BazarImportAction object-injection exploit request (CVE-2026-52777) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the YesWiki BazaR importer endpoint (?BazaR&vue=importer) that carry the vulnerable importfiche parameter, the exact request shape an attacker uses to reach the unserialize() sink in CSVManager.php. Article-specific because it keys on YesWiki's own routing string rather than a generic deserialization pattern. Rationale: Uses YesWiki's exact routing tokens BazaR + vue=importer (from BazarAction::run VOIR_IMPORTER -> callAction('bazarimport')) plus POST method, which is the only path that reaches CSVManager::importEntry. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and YesWiki issue #356. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/issues/356
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using the Bazar CSV import UI to import entries
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Burp) probing the importer endpoint
  • Security team validating the CVE-2026-52777 patch on 4.6.6
  • Automated content-migration scripts that POST to the importer
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors that replay a saved import request
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "Nuclei" and csUserAgent !has "Burp" and cIP !in ("<known-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matched cIP/csUserName; confirm request body contained importfiche[] and whether the source is an internal admin workstation or an external/unknown IP, and check the Referer for a cross-site origin (CSRF). 2) Contain: if body carried a base64 blob or the source is untrusted, block the source IP at the WAF and force-logout/rotate the admin session; verify the host is on YesWiki >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: search same host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells and for wakka.config.php or *.php writes under the webroot in the following 30 minutes.

| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=importer"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserName, scStatus, csUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Base64 PHP-serialized-object payload in importfiche POST body AIExploitation High
Detects the deserialization payload itself: a request to a YesWiki host whose body contains the importfiche parameter alongside a base64 string that decodes to a PHP serialized object (prefixes Tzo = 'O:' object, YToxOnt = 'a:1:{' array as in the PoC). This is the highest-fidelity signal that an actual object-injection payload (e.g. a PHPGGC Doctrine chain) was sent, not just endpoint probing. Rationale: Combines the article's exact sink-feeding param name (importfiche, from BazarImportAction formatArguments) with base64 markers of PHP serialization grammar (Tzo/YToxOnt) exercised by base64_decode+unserialize; the PoC payload itself begins YToxOnt. Requires a WAF that logs the POST body, noted as a deployment prerequisite. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb

  • Security researcher submitting benign serialized test objects
  • Pen-test / red-team validating CVE-2026-52777 with PHPGGC
  • WAF replaying a captured malicious request during tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: base64-decode the matched importfiche value; if it decodes to O:<n>:"<Class>" confirm the class (e.g. Doctrine\*) and whether it is a known PHPGGC gadget. 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF, isolate the YesWiki host pending review, and rotate the targeted admin session/credentials; patch to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: on the host, look for php-fpm/apache child shells, new webshells under the webroot, and outbound connections initiated by the web-server user in the minutes after the request.

YesWiki web-server process spawning an OS shell (deserialization RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the payoff of a successful PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 chain: the YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm/apache2/httpd/nginx) spawning a shell or download/exec utility. On a normal YesWiki host these processes never fork /bin/sh, curl, wget or python. Rationale: The article states Doctrine/RCE1 terminates in system($cmd); the observable is the web-server process forking a shell/downloader, which on a PHP wiki host is essentially never benign. Parent set (php-fpm/apache2/httpd/nginx) is article/stack-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A YesWiki plugin/cron legitimately shelling out via exec() (e.g. image conversion via ImageMagick/convert)
  • Deployment or backup scripts run under the web-server user
  • Composer/npm build steps executed by the web account during updates
  • Health-check scripts invoking curl from the app tier
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "ImageMagick" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/usr/bin/convert" and not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has "healthcheck")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the php-fpm parent; determine if it maps to a known plugin/cron or is an ad-hoc shell (id/whoami/reverse-shell). 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and preserve the php-fpm worker for forensics; block any C2 IP seen. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web-server user (webshells, wakka.config.php), review MySQL access, and pivot to other sites on the same shared host.

YesWiki wakka.config.php modified by web-server account (post-RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Alerts when YesWiki's core config file wakka.config.php is created/modified by a web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx). The advisory names wakka.config.php as an explicit post-exploitation target; that file is not rewritten by the web tier during normal operation, so a web-server-initiated write is a strong persistence/tamper signal. Rationale: Advisory Impact section explicitly lists modifying wakka.config.php as an attacker post-exploitation action; the file+web-process-initiator pairing is high-fidelity because the web tier does not rewrite core config in normal use. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running the YesWiki installer/updater under the web-server user which rewrites wakka.config.php
  • A legitimate config-change action performed through the wiki admin UI
  • Automated provisioning/IaC re-templating the config file
  • Migration to 4.6.6 that touches the config during upgrade
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "install" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "update" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "upgrade"
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the new wakka.config.php against the last known-good version; check for injected PHP, altered DB creds, or debug/eval flags, and correlate with an importfiche POST in the prior 30 min. 2) Contain: restore the vetted config, isolate the host, and rotate DB and admin credentials; upgrade to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: scan the webroot for newly written *.php (webshells), review recent web-server-spawned processes, and inspect MySQL for unauthorized dumps.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wakka.config.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName has "wakka.config.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki unauthenticated erasespamedcomments page-deletion invocation (CVE-2026-52766) AIExploitation High
Hunts POST requests to a YesWiki instance that reference the `erasespamedcomments` action together with the `clean`/`suppr[]` deletion parameters, the exact request shape from the CVE-2026-52766 PoC. Because the action performs no authorization or CSRF check, any single such request from an unauthenticated source is a live exploitation attempt for arbitrary wiki page deletion (including PagePrincipale). Rationale: Uses the CVE-specific action name `erasespamedcomments` plus the `suppr[]`/`clean=yes` deletion parameters from the advisory PoC (POST /?wiki=SpamCleanup, clean=yes&suppr[0]=...). The action name is unique to YesWiki and the parameter trio is otherwise never seen, giving a near-zero-FP signature; requires a log source that captures POST body/full query (WAF or app log) since IIS alone omits the body. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated wiki admin legitimately running spam-comment cleanup after a spam wave
  • Security scanner / DAST tool (Burp, Nuclei) firing a CVE-2026-52766 test request in an authorized pentest
  • Vulnerability-management team validating the patch on a staging YesWiki host
  • A WAF replay/allow-list health check that reissues a captured deletion request
Suppression filter
| where csUserName == "" or isempty(csUserName)   // keep only unauthenticated callers; authenticated admin cleanup is expected
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matching cIP/src — confirm it is unauthenticated (empty csUserName) and enumerate the tags inside suppr[]; check whether PagePrincipale or admin pages are named. 2) Contain: if unauthenticated and unexpected, block the source IP at the WAF, put the YesWiki instance into hibernation (WIKI_IN_HIBERNATION) or take it offline, and confirm the app is upgraded to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: search all access logs from the same src for the preceding trigger-page creation (POST to */edit carrying {{erasespamedcomments}}) and for a 404 spike on the deleted tags; restore affected pages from DB/page-history backup.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "erasespamedcomments" or csUriQuery has_any ("erasespamedcomments","suppr","clean=yes")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, sSiteName, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserName, csUserAgent, Computer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki confirmed mass page deletion — bulk 'Suppression de la page' / deletion-request burst (CVE-2026-52766) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the impact stage of CVE-2026-52766: a burst of confirmed page deletions in a short window, either as YesWiki admin-log 'Suppression de la page' entries (application log) or as a spike of erasespamedcomments/suppr deletion POSTs from one source. Legitimate admin cleanup touches 1-3 pages; mass abuse deletes many tags in one automated run. Rationale: Pivots on the exact admin-log string `Suppression de la page` written by PageController::delete()->LogAdministrativeAction (article code), and on a per-source burst of suppr/erasespamedcomments POSTs. Volume + the CVE-specific action string separates automated mass deletion from routine single-page maintenance; the app-log path also confirms deletions actually succeeded rather than merely being attempted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wiki admin performing a large legitimate content purge/migration (decommissioning a namespace)
  • Scripted maintenance job that deletes stale pages in bulk on a schedule
  • Restore/reimport operation that deletes-then-recreates many pages
  • Spam wave genuinely being cleaned by an authorized moderator using the intended feature
Response runbook
1) Triage: expand the make_set of SamplePages / suppr tags to see which pages were deleted and whether PagePrincipale, admin, or other users' pages are included; correlate to the source IP and whether it was authenticated. 2) Contain: hibernate or isolate the YesWiki host, block the source IP, and confirm the upgrade to >=4.6.6 (or apply an ACL gating erasespamedcomments to admins). 3) Hunt: pull page-history/DB backups and restore deleted tags; check for the initial trigger-page creation and for follow-on defacement or re-creation of the front page by the same source.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "Suppression de la page"
| summarize DeletedPages = count(), SamplePages = make_set(SyslogMessage, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by HostName, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DeletedPages > 5   // >5 confirmed page deletions in a 10-min window — far above manual admin cleanup (typ. 1-3)
| order by DeletedPages desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count > 5
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST AND (Web.url="*erasespamedcomments*" OR Web.uri_query="*erasespamedcomments*" OR Web.uri_query="*suppr*" OR Web.url="*suppr*") by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=10m

YesWiki page-deletion aftermath — 404 spike on previously-valid wiki pages (CVE-2026-52766) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream impact of CVE-2026-52766: pages deleted by the erasespamedcomments abuse now return HTTP 404 to normal visitors. A sudden spike of 404s across many distinct wiki page paths in a short window — especially minutes after an erasespamedcomments POST — indicates successful mass deletion. Rationale: Uses the YesWiki URL shape (`?wiki=<PageTag>`) plus a 404 status spike across many distinct page tags, which is the observable end state after PageManager::deleteOrphaned() wipes pages/links/acls/tags rows. Best deployed as a same-source time-window correlation with UC1's erasespamedcomments POST to cut ambiguity from ordinary broken-link 404s. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Broken-link crawler / SEO bot hitting many stale URLs
  • Legitimate content restructure where pages were intentionally renamed or removed
  • A vulnerability scanner enumerating non-existent wiki page tags
  • Cache/CDN warm-up requesting pages that legitimately never existed
Suppression filter
| where csUriStem has_any ("wiki") | where DistinctPages > 10 and NotFound > 20   // require both breadth (distinct pages) and volume to suppress lone broken-link crawlers
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct 404 page tags and check whether any were serving 200 in the hours before the spike (a genuine deletion signature) versus never-existed paths (scanner noise). 2) Contain: if prior-200 pages are now 404, treat as confirmed destruction — isolate the host, block the abusing source from UC1/UC2, and confirm patch >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: correlate the 404 tags to the suppr[] array values in the preceding erasespamedcomments POST from the same window/source, then restore the affected pages from backup and monitor for re-deletion.
W3CIISLog

| where scStatus == 404
| where csUriStem has "wiki" or csUriQuery has "wiki"
| summarize NotFound = count(), DistinctPages = dcount(csUriQuery), Pages = make_set(csUriQuery, 50) by Computer, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DistinctPages > 10   // >10 distinct previously-served wiki pages now 404 in a 15-min window — deletion aftermath
| order by NotFound desc

UAT-7810 ORB relay C2 — outbound to LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH relay IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts internal hosts or edge devices establishing outbound sessions to the four hard IP indicators Talos attributes to UAT-7810's ORB relay/C2 infrastructure. Article-specific because it pins to the exact relay IPs, not a generic beacon heuristic. Rationale: Uses the four concrete relay IPs (194.233.92.26, 217.15.160.247, 217.15.164.147, 95.182.100.231) named in the Talos IOC set — hard indicators, so any hit is high-fidelity regardless of process context.

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Security researcher/VM sandbox detonating a sample toward the IPs
  • Shared cloud/CDN re-allocation of the IP to a benign tenant after the campaign
  • Perimeter proxy logging the connection on behalf of a blocked client

| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal src_ip/DeviceName and the initiating process; confirm the IP is still on the Talos block/IOC list and not re-allocated. 2) Contain: block the four IPs at egress, isolate the host if a non-security process initiated the traffic, and preserve netflow. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the four prevalent-malware SHA256s, check whether the device is a Ruckus/ASUS edge appliance being recruited as a relay node, and review inbound sessions from the same IP range.

Unpatched Ruckus/ASUS edge devices exposed to UAT-7810 exploit CVEs AIExploitation High
Surfaces network/edge devices in inventory that carry the exact Ruckus and ASUS CVEs UAT-7810 exploits for initial access into ORB nodes. Article-specific because it pins to the four named CVEs rather than generic router risk. Rationale: Pins to CVE-2020-22653, CVE-2020-22658, CVE-2023-25717 (Ruckus) and CVE-2025-2492 (ASUS) — the specific n-day vulns Talos says UAT-7810 exploits to build ORB nodes; exposure hunting is the executable form since no exploit payload strings were published.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Isolated management-VLAN router not internet-reachable (lower real risk)

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged device is a live, internet-reachable Ruckus/ASUS edge unit and validate the firmware version against the vendor fixed release. 2) Contain: schedule/apply the firmware update or ACL the WAN management interface; if patching is delayed, restrict mgmt ports (80/443/8080) to admin subnets. 3) Hunt: check egress from that device to the four ORB relay IPs and for new admin accounts or config changes indicating prior compromise.

Talos prevalent-malware SHA256 execution (UAT-7810 telemetry batch) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on execution of any file matching the four SHA256 hashes listed in the Talos report's most-prevalent-malware section. Article-specific: exact hashes, so any match is a confirmed known-bad binary. Rationale: Uses the four exact SHA256 values published by Talos (VID001.exe coinminer, SECOH-QAD.exe procpatcher, etc.). These are the article's most-prevalent-malware batch; hash matches are unambiguous known-bad, though attribution to LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH is not confirmed by Talos.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • IR responder copying the sample onto a forensic host for analysis
  • EDR/AV quarantine relocation event re-hashing the file
  • Threat-intel enrichment tool staging the sample for detonation
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-sandbox01","ir-forensics01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 hit, the executing user/host, and whether the host is a sanctioned analysis VM. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the binary; block the hashes org-wide. 3) Hunt: pivot the host for outbound to the four ORB relay IPs, check autoruns/services for SECOH-QAD.exe (procpatcher) persistence, and sweep the estate for the same hashes.

Edge device recruited as ORB relay — inbound sessions from UAT-7810 IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects internal hosts or edge appliances ACCEPTING inbound connections from the four UAT-7810 relay IPs — the signature of a node being used as an ORB proxy conduit for secondary APT traffic, distinct from outbound beaconing. Rationale: Same four relay IPs but pivots on the INBOUND direction — matches the article's core thesis that UAT-7810 turns edge devices into relay nodes routing secondary-actor traffic; a device accepting sessions from these IPs is likely a recruited ORB node.
ATT&CKT1133 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate inbound service (VPN/remote-mgmt) that the IP was temporarily reassigned to
  • Firewall logging a blocked inbound attempt (still worth review but not a compromise)
  • Internet background-radiation scan hitting an exposed port
  • Threat-intel honeypot deliberately accepting the connection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection was ACCEPTED (not blocked) and identify the listening service/port and the receiving host role. 2) Contain: ACL the four IPs inbound, isolate the device if it is not a designed remote-access endpoint, and capture the listening process. 3) Hunt: inspect the host for proxy/tunnel tooling, correlate with outbound sessions to different downstream targets (relay-through pattern), and review config for unauthorized port-forward rules.

| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count() by DeviceName, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/network activity to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network, the character-code-rebuilt exfil host used by the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 to smuggle base64 wallet key material inside an X-Request-Id header disguised as gRPC-web traffic. Article-specific because the FQDN is a fixed IOC unique to this campaign. Rationale: The exfil FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is a fixed, campaign-unique IOC (a lookalike subdomain never served by real Injective infra); matching it exactly avoids the FP risk of the parent injective.network.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1132.001 T1041 T1001.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate future Injective testnet archival endpoint being stood up under this exact FQDN (verify DNS/PKI ownership)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the malicious package intentionally
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or research VM deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Internal DNS logging replaying old cached queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving host ran an @injectivelabs-dependent app; capture the initiating process (node.exe) and user. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat every wallet mnemonic/private key derived on it as exposed — freeze/rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts querying the FQDN, pull package-lock/yarn.lock for @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21, and search DeviceFileEvents for the two malicious build artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk AIInstallation Medium
Detects the two poisoned build files (accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) from @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 landing on disk, matched on their exact SHA-256 hashes. High fidelity IOC match that survives file renaming. Rationale: Both SHA-256 values are published IOCs for the exact malicious build artifacts; a hash match is unambiguous and near-zero FP, catching the stealer even if the file is renamed during transitive install.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware analyst intentionally storing the sample
  • Backup or EDR quarantine copy of the artifact triggering a second file event
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion writing the IOC file to a sandbox share
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and host; confirm whether it is a dev/CI machine or an analyst sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the affected node_modules, and pin @injectivelabs/* to a clean version (>=1.20.23); treat any wallet keys handled on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints/CI runners for the same hashes and for outbound contact to the exfil FQDN.

Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Structural supply-chain detection: the campaign-unique build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js appearing under a node_modules/@injectivelabs path. Resilient to re-signing/re-hash because it keys on the version-marker filenames + package scope rather than the SHA-256, catching victims who pulled the stealer transitively via any of the 18 sibling packages. Rationale: The build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js are unique to the poisoned 1.20.21 dist and act as a version marker; combined with the node_modules/@injectivelabs scope this flags transitive victims (e.g. via wallet-core) who never named sdk-ts directly, and survives re-hash of the still-downloadable deprecated package.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Aikido/other scanner replaying the artifact during a rescan
  • Developer intentionally checking out the compromised version to reproduce/analyze
  • A future clean @injectivelabs build coincidentally reusing the same hashed chunk name (unlikely — Rollup chunk hashes are content-derived)
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read the package's package.json version and lockfile to confirm 1.20.21 was resolved (directly or transitively). 2) Contain: delete node_modules, repin @injectivelabs/* to >=1.20.23, and rebuild; flag any wallet keys/seed phrases derived on the host for rotation. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/CI job with @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21 in lockfiles and correlate hosts against exfil-domain contacts and the SHA-256 file detection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "injectivelabs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "injectivelabs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — One Target, Two Flags | Rival Espionage Actors Converge On Pakistani Law Enforce
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement · [LLM] Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement AICommand & Control High
Hunts any internal host establishing outbound connections to the 13 C2 IPs SentinelLABS attributed to the four tooling clusters (PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, Remcos) converging on Balochistan Police and other Pakistani law-enforcement orgs between Feb 2024 and Apr 2026. Pure network-IOC match on disclosed espionage C2 servers. Rationale: Anchored on the exact 13 C2 IPs from Table 1 / code blocks (PlugX 172.111.233.x + 172.94.9.x + 45.74.6.17, ShadowPad 45.125.32.218, Cobalt Strike 142.171.183.8 + 193.42.25.65, Remcos 89.31.121.220). Any egress to these known-bad hosts is high-fidelity; the tooling families and Pakistani-entity victimology are corroborated externally, though the specific IPs are from the SentinelLABS primary report only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad • https://thehackernews.com/2023/07/pakistani-entities-targeted-in.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately sandboxing or sinkholing one of these IPs from a corporate host
  • IP reassignment after takedown — a benign service later hosted on a recycled VPS IP (172.94.9.x / 45.x hosting ranges are commodity VPS)
  • Internal threat-intel validation tooling or EDR connectivity checks pinging the IOC list
  • Proxy/NAT concentration causing many internal hosts to appear as one src toward the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR/AV connectivity-check processes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection is genuinely outbound and established (not a blocked/attempt), identify the initiating process and host role — servers hosting the CMS/FIR/HRMIS/HotelEye/CRMS apps are highest priority. 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at perimeter, isolate the host, snapshot memory before reboot to preserve PlugX/ShadowPad in-memory implants. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DLL side-loading (unsigned DLL next to a signed EXE), scheduled tasks/Run keys created near first-seen, and lateral SMB/RDP from the host; sweep the org for any other host touching the same /24s (172.111.233.0/24, 172.94.9.0/24).
let C2 = dynamic(["172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17","45.125.32.218","142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","89.31.121.220"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
let C2 = dynamic(["172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17","45.125.32.218","142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","89.31.121.220"]);
ImNetworkSession

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber, 20) by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by LastSeen desc

Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) AICommand & Control Medium
Tighter server-side pivot: a web/application-server process (IIS w3wp, Apache/Tomcat java, nginx, php-cgi) on a Pakistani law-enforcement web server initiating outbound to the disclosed C2 IPs. Grounds on the article's China-nexus 'custom implants masquerading as a portal update' planted in one of the citizen/police web applications (e.g. the Complaint Management System). Rationale: Combines the exact C2 IP set with a server-process filter to isolate the article's specific scenario — a China-nexus implant planted in a citizen/police web application (CMS) beaconing out. Web-server processes reaching commodity-VPS C2 IPs is extremely rare and high-fidelity, and directly targets the compromised-webapp vector the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1505.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately calling an outbound API that happens to be on a recycled VPS IP after IOC takedown
  • Java-based agent/monitoring on the web server making outbound telemetry calls
  • Server-side update/package fetch (Tomcat/Maven, php composer) to a mirror on the same hosting range
  • App-server health-check or CDN origin-pull to a reassigned address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "maven" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "composer" // exclude server package-manager fetches
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which web application the process serves (CMS/FIR/HRMIS/AVLS/HotelEye/CRMS) and whether the beacon started after a recent 'portal update'/deployment window; review web-root for recently modified/added handler, JSP, ASPX or PHP files. 2) Contain: take the web app offline or block egress, preserve IIS/Tomcat logs and web-root for forensics, rotate app/service and DB credentials the server can reach. 3) Hunt: search web access logs (W3CIISLog/AppServiceHTTPLogs) for the implant's request pattern, look for webshell-style POSTs, and pivot to any DB export or biometric/criminal-record access from the compromised app identity.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17", "45.125.32.218", "142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "89.31.121.220") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17", "45.125.32.218", "142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "89.31.121.220"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
